papers.title_in_file: Better than classical? The subtle art of benchmarking quantum machine learning models
papers.version_note: arXiv:2403.07059v2 [quant-ph], 14 Mar 2024 (dated March 15, 2024). The text layer holds the paper once.
papers.what_it_is: A large-scale benchmark study from Xanadu that tests 12 prototypical quantum machine learning models against classical baselines on 160 mostly synthetic binary classification datasets, with ablations that remove entanglement and a discussion of benchmarking pitfalls.

existing.note: The paper limits the result: not all models were tested on all datasets and benchmarks (runtime limits), and the finding holds for the small-scale datasets chosen. The abstract's wording 6 binary classification tasks creating 160 datasets is the paper's own; Section III calls the 6 items data generation procedures grouped into 10 benchmarks.
existing.value: The authors report that in a benchmark of 12 quantum machine learning models on 6 binary classification tasks creating 160 datasets, out-of-the-box classical machine learning models outperform the quantum classifiers overall; they note that not all models are tested on all datasets and benchmarks.
existing.anchor: Abstract, p.1; Section V.A, p.14; Introduction, p.2
quotes: We find that overall, out-of-the-box classical machine learning models outperform the quantum classifiers.
systematically tests 12 popular quantum machine learning models on 6 binary classification tasks used to create 160 individual datasets
Note that not all models are tested on all datasets and benchmarks
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

existing.value: The authors state that they predominantly use artificially generated data, which may limit conclusions with respect to real-world data, and that the largest circuit simulated has 18 qubits.
quotes: we predominantly use artificially generated data which allows us to understand and vary the properties and size of the datasets. This may limit conclusions with respect to “real-world” data
The largest size of a circuit simulated in the study has 18 qubits
existing.certainty_reason: The paper states its own data scope in Section III and the qubit limit in footnote 3.
existing.reader_inference: MNIST (a real dataset, downscaled) is one of the six data generation procedures, so predominantly is the paper's word, not entirely.

existing.note: The result is model dependent. Removing entanglement did not reduce accuracy of DressedQuantumCircuitClassifier, but did reduce it for QuantumBoltzmannMachine and DataReuploadingClassifier. The test was run on mnist pca up to 9 dimensions for the three QNN models that beat the separable model.
existing.value: The authors report that removing entanglement from a quantum model often results in as good or better performance, but that removing entanglement does decrease the test accuracy of QuantumBoltzmannMachine and DataReuploadingClassifier.
existing.anchor: Abstract, p.1; Section V.C, pp.15-17; Fig. 13, p.17
quotes: removing entanglement from a quantum model often results in as good or better performance
However, removing entanglement does decrease the test accuracy of QuantumBoltzmannMachine and DataReuploadingClassifier.
The DressedQuantumCircuitClassifier shows no drop in performance, while DataReuploadingClassifier, and to some extent QuantumBoltzmannMachine, do worse without entanglement.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

existing.note: Section V.B adds that on two curves diff the quantum models perform worse than the classical method as difficulty is increased, and that the claim rests on the difficulty-controlled benchmarks hyperplanes diff, hidden manifold diff and two curves diff.
existing.value: The authors report that they do not observe any improvement in performance of the quantum models relative to the classical baselines for increasing problem difficulties; on two curves diff the quantum models perform worse than the corresponding classical method as the difficulty is increased.
quotes: Secondly, we do not observe any improvement in performance of the quantum models relative to the classical baselines for increasing problem difficulties.
For the difficulty-controlled benchmark two curves diff (Appendix F), the quantum models perform worse than the corresponding classical method as the difficulty is increased.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that of 55 arXiv papers containing the terms quantum machine learning and outperform in title or abstract, about 40% claim that a quantum model outperforms a classical model, about 50% claim that an improvement to a quantum machine learning method outperforms the original one, and only 3 papers or 4% find that a quantum model does not outperform a classical one.
quotes: Out of 55 relevant papers published on the preprint server arXiv 1 until December 2023 that contain the terms “quantum machine learning” and “outperform” in title or abstract
one finds that about 40% claim that a quantum model outperforms a classical model, while about 50% claim that some improvement to a quantum machine learning method outperforms the original one
Only 3 papers or 4% find that a quantum model does not outperform
assertions.certainty_reason: A literature count by one study; the sample is keyword-selected.
assertions.reader_inference: The count is a snapshot taken until December 2023 and depends on the keyword choice.

assertions.value: The authors state that the 55 papers are a subset of 73 papers returned by the keyword search, selected by manually reading abstracts and discarding papers on quantum-inspired methods, other fields, or without an explicit method-outperforms-method statement; other search terms showed similar patterns.
quotes: The 55 papers are a subset of 73 papers returned by the keyword search, and were selected by manually reading the abstracts
Other search terms than “outperform*”, such as “better than” or “benchmark*”, were tried to detect a possible selection bias caused by the keyword search, but showed similar patterns.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own selection procedure in footnotes 1 and 2.

assertions.value: The authors report a simulated thought experiment in which 100 researchers each investigate 20 quantum models and publish only the best against a classical model; with assumed true performance of mean 0.65 (standard deviation 0.07) for classical and mean 0.55 (standard deviation 0.1) for quantum models, the published mean performance of the quantum models is 0.74 versus 0.65 for classical ones.
quotes: Consider 100 researchers, each investigating 20 different types of quantum models before settling on a promising design and publishing benchmarks of the best one against a classical model of their choice.
(say, with a mean of 0.65 and standard deviation of 0.07) than quantum ones (mean 0.55, standard deviation 0.1)
the published mean performance of the quantum models is 0.74 vs. 0.65 of classical ones
assertions.certainty_reason: A simulation under assumed normal distributions chosen by the authors; an illustration, not a measurement of the field.
assertions.reader_inference: The distribution parameters are assumptions of the authors, so the 0.74 figure illustrates the mechanism and is not an estimate of real published results.

assertions.value: The authors state that a positivity bias of this nature is not a question of ethical misconduct but is built into the research methodology of leaderboard-driven research, and that performance of a model cannot be viewed as a property that can be demonstrated by an empirical study.
quotes: a positivity bias of this nature is not a question of ethical misconduct, but built into the research methodology.
cannot be viewed as a property that can be “demonstrated” by an empirical study
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument by the authors without a measurement beyond the illustration.

assertions.value: The authors report an illustrative example in which a minor rearrangement of the data in a classification task causes an adversarially hand-crafted quantum model to switch from being nearly unable to learn to gaining perfect accuracy.
quotes: a minor rearrangement of the data in a classification task causes an – admittedly adversarially hand-crafted – quantum model to switch from being nearly unable to learn, to gaining perfect accuracy
assertions.certainty_reason: A single hand-crafted example, labeled by the authors as highly simplified.

assertions.value: The paper cites studies reporting that leaderboard rankings change when a few datasets are excluded or scores are aggregated differently (Dehghani et al.), that correcting labeling errors in the ImageNet validation set changes the ranking of models (Northcutt et al.), and that a different test-train split decreases accuracies by as much as 14% (Recht et al.), with the ranking between models largely unaffected by the split.
quotes: significantly different leaderboard rankings are obtained when excluding a few datasets from benchmarking suites or making changes to the way that scores are aggregated
find that correcting labeling errors in the ubiquitous ImageNet validation set likewise changes the ranking of models
decreases the accuracies of models by as much as 14%
Although, reassuringly, the ranking between models is largely unaffected by this intervention.
assertions.certainty_reason: Results the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The paper cites studies suggesting that small adjustments to transformer architectures have no measurable effect on performance, that standard convolutional neural networks still beat transformers when trained on a comparable amount of data, and that extensive hyperparameter optimisation can give baseline models of generative adversarial networks, deep reinforcement learning and Bayesian deep neural nets the performance of more advanced proposals.
quotes: small adjustments to transformer architectures advertised in the literature have no measurable effect on their performance
still beat transformers when trained on a comparable amount of data

extensive hyperparameter optimisation can give baseline models of generative adversarial networks [38], deep reinforcement learning [39] and Bayesian deep neural nets [40] the performance of more advanced proposals
assertions.certainty_reason: Results the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the question Does my quantum model beat classical machine learning is impossible to answer by a numerical experiment, whereas a question of clearly defined scope, such as whether the performance of a model on a specific task increases if the data or training conditions change, might be answerable.
quotes: “Does my quantum model beat classical machine learning?” is impossible to answer by a numerical experiment
“Does the performance of a model on a specific task increase as measured by some metric, if we change the data, or training conditions?” might be.
assertions.certainty_reason: A methodological position of the authors.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's own headline finding that classical models outperform the quantum ones answers a form of the first question for its setting, so the two statements need reading together.

assertions.value: The authors report an analysis of 15 randomly selected papers (out of 46 identified) using MNIST for supervised quantum machine learning benchmarks: more than half use a pre-processing strategy such as resolution reduction or PCA, only four use the original multi-class MNIST problem, and reported accuracies range from 70 to 99.6%.
quotes: a representative analysis of 15 randomly selected papers in quantum machine learning using MNIST benchmarks7 shows that more than half use a pre-processing strategy like resolution reduction or PCA to lower the number of input features
only four of the papers in our representative sample of 15 use the original MNIST multi-class problem
range from accuracies of 70 − 99.6% are mixed and hard to interpret with respect to the known baseline
These were sampled out of 46 papers that we identified to use MNIST for supervised learning benchmarks
assertions.certainty_reason: A literature sample of one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the 2-dimensional PCA-reduced MNIST 3-5 classification problem consists of about 10, 000 datapoints that lie in overlapping blobs, a task that is hardly meaningful, and that downscaling the 784 original pixels to tens of features voids the extensive knowledge about the baseline to beat; they cite Bausch for reducing images to a 4 × 4 resolution leading to 70% of test images also being present during training.
quotes: downscaling the 784 original pixels by that much voids our extensive knowledge about the baseline to beat
the 2-dimensional PCA-reduced MNIST 3-5 classification problem consists of about 10, 000 datapoints that lie in overlapping blobs
as Bausch [47] remarks, reducing images to a 4 × 4 resolution leads to 70% of test images also being present during training
assertions.certainty_reason: An author argument; the Bausch figure is a cited result.

assertions.value: The authors state that the sampled MNIST results collectively do not give convincing evidence for quantum models to systematically reach the test accuracies of 98.6% or even 99.4% put forward by Hinton for the original MNIST task, at least not if unaided by powerful classical models.
quotes: Collectively, they certainly do not give convincing evidence for quantum models to systematically reach the test accuracies of 98.6% or even 99.4% put forward by Hinton with respect to the original MNIST task
assertions.certainty_reason: An author judgment about a literature sample.

assertions.value: The paper quotes Hinton that sensibly-engineered convolutional neural nets with a few hidden layers typically get about 0.6% test error on MNIST, and that feed-forward networks with ReLUs in the permutation-invariant version typically get about 1.4% test error, reducible to around 1.1% with regularizers.
quotes: Sensibly-engineered convolutional neural nets with a few hidden layers typically get about 0.6% test error.
feed-forward neural networks with a few fully connected hidden layers of Rectified Linear Units (ReLUs) typically get about 1.4% test error.
This can be reduced to around 1.1% test error using a variety of regularizers
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Hinton.

assertions.value: The authors state that their arguments put into question the practice of adopting datasets from classical machine learning blindly when their benefits are lost, and that alternatives such as 1-d MNIST may be a lot more suitable; they still add MNIST as a task for comparability with other studies.
quotes: put into question the practice of adopting datasets from classical machine learning blindly when their benefits are lost
Alternatives, such as 1-d MNIST [48] designed to scale down deep learning experiments, may be a lot more suitable.
we will still add MNIST as a task here in order to make our results easier to compare with so many other studies
assertions.certainty_reason: An author position.

assertions.value: The authors state that they selected models in four steps: arXiv quant-ph papers from 1 January 2018 to 1 June 2023 with keywords classif*, learn*, supervised, MNIST (3500 papers); papers with 30 or more Google Scholar citations on 2 June 2023 (561 papers); papers proposing a new quantum model for classification on conventional classical data judged from the abstract (29 papers); a random subset of 15 papers of which four could not reasonably be implemented (11 papers).
quotes: We first collected all papers accessible via the arXiv API in the period 1 January 2018 to 1 June 2023 in the “quant-ph” category
to find the overwhelming share of papers that are part of the current quantum machine learning discourse. [3500 papers]
From the previous set we sub-selected papers with 30 or more Google Scholar citations on the cutoff date 2 June 2023.
It inevitably also biases towards older papers (see Figure 4). [561 papers]
This ensured that the models can be meaningfully compared via a focused set of benchmarks, and that we limit ourselves to original proposals. [29 papers]
we sampled a random subset of 15 papers from the 29 candidates.
After reading the full body of these papers we had to exclude another four that we could not reasonably implement
[11 papers]

assertions.value: The authors state that they do not claim to capture the best or most advanced algorithmic designs but those that are the foundation of models proposed today, and that the citation threshold inevitably biases the selection towards older papers.
quotes: Importantly, we are not claiming to capture the “best” or most advanced algorithmic designs, but rather those that are the foundation of models proposed today.
Selecting papers with 30 or more citations introduces a bias towards less recent work.

assertions.value: The authors state that from the final selection of 11 papers they implemented 12 quantum machine learning models, because Havlicek et al. compared two distinct architectures, both of which they implemented, and that the 12 models split into three families: quantum neural networks, quantum kernel methods and quantum convolutional neural networks.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A, p.5; Section II.B, p.6
quotes: From this final selection of 11 papers [13, 15, 18–20, 51– 56] we implemented 12 quantum machine learning models.
both of which we implemented.

assertions.value: The authors state that they study six quantum neural network classifiers and then describe CircuitCentricClassifier, DataReuploadingClassifier, DressedQuantumCircuitClassifier, IQPVariationalClassifier, QuantumBoltzmannMachine, QuantumMetricLearner and TreeTensorClassifier.
quotes: We study six quantum neural network classifiers:

The choice of loss function for training varies among models9. Two models use a cross entropy loss, three use a square loss, one uses a linear loss, and one uses a loss based on distances between embedded quantum states
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own count disagrees with its own list.
assertions.reader_inference: The list names seven models, and the loss counts (two, three, one, one) also sum to seven. Seven QNNs plus three kernel methods plus two convolutional models give the stated 12 models, so six appears to be a typo for seven.

assertions.value: The authors define a quantum neural network model as one that combines one or more variational quantum circuits, each of the form f(theta, x) = tr[O(x, theta) rho(x, theta)], to classify data into one of two labels y = ±1 through a class prediction function, and note that quantum neural networks are simply variational quantum circuits that encode data and are trainable by gradient-descent methods.
quotes: simply variational quantum circuits that encode data and are trainable by gradientdescent methods

For our purposes, a quantum neural network model is one that combines one or more such variational quantum circuits {f1, ..., fL} to classify data into one of two labels y = ±1 through a class prediction function fpred:
assertions.certainty_reason: A definition stated by the paper in Section II.B.1.

assertions.value: The authors define a quantum kernel method as one in which the kernel function is evaluated with the aid of a quantum computer, commonly by embedding the classical data into quantum states rho(x) and using the kernel k(xi, xj) = tr[rho(xi) rho(xj)].
quotes: A quantum kernel method is one in which the kernel function is evaluated with the aid of a quantum computer.
which is a kernel by virtue of being an inner product, and can be evaluated by methods that evaluate state overlaps.
assertions.certainty_reason: A definition stated by the paper in Section II.B.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that they do not capture quantum convolutional models in a strict mathematical definition but identify them as quantum neural network models that, like classical convolutional models, exploit a form of translation symmetry, and that they study two such models, QuanvolutionalNeuralNetwork and WeiNet.

We study two such models:
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own working definition in Section II.B.3.

assertions.value: The authors state in Section II.B that QuantumKitchenSinks is loosely included among the quantum kernel methods and that its implementation does use a SVM as in the other two models, and state in Appendix C that the feature mapped vectors are passed to a linear classifier implemented using scikit-learn’s LogisticRegression class.

assertions.value: The authors state that the classical baselines are a standard feed-forward neural network (scikit-learn MLPClassifier), a support vector classifier with Gaussian kernel (scikit-learn SVC) and a convolutional neural network (ConvolutionalNeuralNetwork, implemented using Flax), chosen as out-of-the-box versions that are not intended to be state-of-the-art models.

The first two of these were implemented using scikit-learn’s MLPClassifier and SVC classes, and the third that we call ConvolutionalNeuralNetwork was implemented using Flax [68].

assertions.value: The authors state three principles for dataset choice: predominantly artificially generated data to vary properties and size, maximal diversity of datasets through fundamentally different generators, and, in the last three of six data generation procedures, the manifold hypothesis that typical data effectively lives on low-dimensional manifolds; they do not claim to answer which data suits quantum models.
quotes: We followed three overarching principles: Firstly, we predominantly use artificially generated data which allows us to understand and vary the properties and size of the datasets.
Secondly, we aim at maximising the diversity of the datasets by using fundamentally different functional relationships and procedures as generators
Thirdly, in the last three out of six data generation procedures introduced below we follow the “manifold hypothesis” [74–76]
While we do not claim to provide satisfying answers to these questions
